source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Carvalho_2019_LancetSeminarAUD.pdf, Lancet 2019;394:781–92. All 12 pages were read in a -layout text extraction: summary, search box, all sections, the Colombia panel, Tables 1 and 2 (doses not recorded), the captions of Figures 1 and 2, declarations, acknowledgments and all 140 references. Pp. 782, 784, 785, 787 and 789 were checked on pages rendered at 200 dpi, and all pages were viewed at 110 dpi. Figure 1 (world map) was read from its legend; the USA's band was identified by matching pixel colours to the legend swatches. The reference list was re-parsed by column to check the card's counts. The online appendix is not on file and was not read.

claims.overstatement: None. The WHO figures are presented as estimates, attributed to the review, called second-hand, and the review's 'rough estimates' caveat is kept.
claims.note: Every number from this source matches the rendered p. 782: 2016, men 8.6% (95% CI 8.1–9.1), women 1.7% (1.6–1.9), total 5.1% (4.9–5.4); high-income countries 8.4% (8.0–8.9), upper-middle-income 5.4% (5.0–6.0), both sexes combined. The figures are cited to WHO's Global status report on alcohol and health 2018 (ref 1) and Rehm & Shield 2019 (ref 2); the income-group figures to ref 1 only. 'Aged 15 or older' is stated in the same paragraph for the country overview (Figure 1). The reason the authors give for 'rough estimates': several criteria are culturally specific, and the figures come from general population surveys (ref 28, by the senior author). No editors' calculation from this source. Two qualifiers the editor may want. (1) The Seminar does not say which case definition or time window the WHO figures use. The authors' own working definition of alcohol use disorder equals moderate-to-severe DSM-5 disorder or ICD-11 dependence, and they call the DSM-5/ICD-11 gap problematic (p. 781). So the WHO world figure and the DSM-5 NESARC-III figures in the same claim are not on one definition. This matters because about half the NESARC-III past-year cases were mild. (2) Figure 1 colours the USA in the 10.1–15.0% band (my reading of the map's legend colours; the Seminar gives no country values). The WHO-based 2016 figure for the USA is therefore closer to the NESARC-III 13.9 than to the other survey's 7.0. This bears on the claim's sentence that the figures depend on the survey.

anchors.extracted: Alcohol use disorders in 2016: men 8.6% (95% CI 8.1–9.1), women 1.7% (1.6–1.9), total 5.1% (4.9–5.4) (refs 1, WHO 2018 global status report, and 2, Rehm & Shield 2019). Men's prevalence five times women's, with signs of the gap narrowing. Highest in high-income (8.4%, 8.0–8.9) and upper-middle-income countries (5.4%, 5.0–6.0), both sexes. Country overview for adults aged 15 and older in Figure 1. Because several criteria are culturally specific, these survey-based figures should be considered rough estimates (ref 28).

DSM-5 diagnoses the disorder when more than one criterion is met, with severity by number of criteria. ICD-11 separates alcohol dependence from a harmful pattern of use, and the authors call the widening DSM-5/ICD-11 gap problematic. Sharing reservations about DSM-5, they use the term alcohol use disorder for compulsive heavy use with loss of control, which they equate with moderate-to-severe DSM-5 disorder or ICD-11 dependence. The definition behind the WHO figures is not stated.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim keeps the review's wording ('received interventions'), dates the global overview to 2004 and calls both figures second-hand.
claims.note: The numbers match the rendered p. 784: more than 13 000 patients and 358 general practitioners in regions of six European countries; 22.3% of patients identified with alcohol dependence received interventions (ref 70); a global treatment prevalence of 21.9% in what the review calls the most recent overview (ref 72, Kohn, Saxena, Levav & Saraceno, Bull World Health Organ 2004, so the claim's 2004 is correct). The declarations on p. 789 match the claim's parenthesis: MH reports personal fees from BrainsWay Technologies, Indivior and Aelis Farma and other income from Pfizer and Adial Pharmaceuticals; JR reports grants from Lundbeck and D&A Pharma; both outside the submitted work. No editors' calculation from this source. Qualifiers the claim could add. (a) The European figure comes from a study led by the Seminar's corresponding author (ref 70: Rehm, Allamani, Della Vedova et al., Ann Fam Med 2015). (b) The review does not say who identified the dependence. In the same study, general practitioners recognised only 30.3% (27.1–33.7) of patients with an instrument-identified disorder, and the instruments found 39.9% (36.0–43.9) of the patients with dependence identified by the GPs (authors' own calculation; p. 785). (c) One sentence of the review contradicts itself: it says the low European rate is not common in other regions, then that the global rate was almost the same. Claims should rest on the figures, as this one does. Consistent with the claim's US figures and severity gradient: the review says US treatment rates were even lower (refs 73, 74), and that people who receive treatment show more drinking, comorbidity, social disintegration and functional loss than those who do not (p. 784). Context for reading any treatment gap: the review notes that a substantial proportion of people recover with no or minimal treatment (p. 784, citing a model caveat) and that an important proportion of these disorders improve without formal intervention (p. 787, ref 110). Not used by the claim: medicines reach an estimated 0.07% of people with the disorder overall and 5.8% of those in specialty treatment, a figure from one 2010 US Veterans Health Administration study (p. 787, ref 109).

anchors.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 1st paragraph (bottom of left column, continued at top of right column)
anchors.extracted: Large study of representative samples of more than 13 000 patients and 358 general practitioners in regions of six European countries: 22.3% of patients identified with alcohol dependence received interventions (ref 70, Rehm et al. 2015). Global treatment prevalence in the most recent overview almost the same, 21.9% (ref 72, Kohn et al. 2004); some countries, such as the USA, lower still (refs 73, 74). The authors infer a treatment gap larger than for any other mental disorder (ref 72). The preceding sentence says the low European rate is not common in other regions, which the next sentence contradicts.

anchors.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 5th paragraph (begins p. 784, figures on p. 785)
anchors.extracted: In the six-country study, GPs relied on drinking level and signs (breath, red eyes, raised liver enzymes) rather than criteria. They identified 30.3% (95% CI 27.1–33.7) of patients with an alcohol use disorder identified by standardised instruments; the instruments identified 39.9% (36.0–43.9) of patients with alcohol dependence identified by GPs (authors' own calculations from ref 70). So the denominator of the 22.3% (patients identified with alcohol dependence) depends on who did the identifying, which the review does not say.

anchors.locator: Clinical presentation and treatment use, 2nd paragraph (p. 784); Genetics and other risk factors, 10th paragraph (p. 784); Acute and long-term management, 1st paragraph (p. 787)
anchors.extracted: Treatment is sought late; compared with people not treated, those treated show higher levels of social disintegration, drinking, comorbidity and functional loss (refs 77, 70); fear of stigma is associated with decreased access (ref 78). A substantial proportion of people recover with no or minimal treatment (p. 784), and an important proportion of alcohol use disorders improve without formal intervention (p. 787, ref 110).

key_findings.correction: In the panel, the attribution to directors of treatment institutions qualifies only the statement that most people with alcohol use disorders refused to be treated together with people who use other drugs. That the alcohol-only inpatient facilities remained almost empty as of May 2019 is the authors' own statement, with no attribution (p. 788, Panel, 3rd and 4th paragraphs). The card's exposure.polysubstance field attributes it correctly. The rest of the finding is confirmed.

missed: Figure 1 (p. 782): the contiguous USA is coloured in the 10.1–15.0% band. I placed it by matching its colour to the legend swatches; no country values are printed. The WHO-based 2016 estimate the Seminar maps for the USA is therefore well above the 7.0% of the US household survey the prevalence claim cites, and close to NESARC-III's 13.9%. This is useful context for the claim's statement that the figures depend on the survey.
